bodyText:
Definition and Origin

Von Neumann architecture, also called the stored-program architecture, is a computer design in which both program instructions and data are stored in the same memory and are processed by a central processing unit. It is named after the mathematician John von Neumann, who described the design in the 1945 report First Draft of a Report on the EDVAC (Electronic Discrete Variable Automatic Computer). The EDVAC itself became operational in the early 1950s. Almost all modern general-purpose computers are based on this architecture.

Main Components

The architecture has four main components. The central processing unit (CPU) executes instructions and is divided into the arithmetic logic unit (ALU), which performs arithmetic and logical operations, and the control unit (CU), which fetches, decodes and coordinates instructions. The memory unit stores both instructions and data. Input and output devices allow the computer to communicate with the outside world. These components are connected by buses: the data bus carries data, the address bus carries memory addresses, and the control bus carries control signals.

The Stored-Program Concept

The central idea is that a program is stored in memory as a sequence of instructions, just like data. Because instructions are treated as data, a program can be loaded, changed and re-run without rewiring the machine. This makes the computer general-purpose rather than built for a single task. The CPU works in a repeating instruction cycle: fetch an instruction from memory, decode it, execute it, and store the result.

The Von Neumann Bottleneck

A major limitation is the Von Neumann bottleneck: the CPU and memory are connected by a single bus, so instructions and data must travel one at a time between them. The CPU often waits for memory, which limits overall speed even when the processor itself is fast. Modern designs reduce this problem with cache memory, wider buses and faster memory, but the basic bottleneck remains a characteristic of the architecture.

Comparison with Harvard Architecture

In the Harvard architecture, instructions and data are stored in separate memories with separate buses, so they can be fetched at the same time. Many microcontrollers and digital signal processors use a modified Harvard architecture, combining separate caches for instructions and data with a unified main memory. Von Neumann architecture remains dominant for general-purpose computers because a single unified memory is simpler and more flexible.

bodyText:
Definition

An instruction set architecture (ISA) is the interface between software and hardware. It defines the set of instructions a processor can execute, the formats of those instructions, the registers available to programmers, the data types supported, and the addressing modes used to access operands. Programs written for one ISA generally cannot run directly on a processor built for a different ISA without recompilation or translation. The ISA is an abstract specification, while the microarchitecture is the actual hardware implementation of that specification.

Instruction Format

Every instruction typically contains an opcode, which specifies the operation to be performed, and one or more operands, which are the data or addresses the operation acts on. For example, an ADD instruction has an opcode for addition and operands naming the registers or memory locations to be added. Instruction length may be fixed, as in many RISC designs, or variable, as in the x86 family. Fixed-length instructions are simpler and faster to decode, while variable-length instructions use memory more compactly.

Types of Instructions

Instructions fall into several broad categories. Data transfer instructions move data between registers and memory, such as LOAD and STORE. Arithmetic and logical instructions perform calculations and comparisons, such as ADD, SUBTRACT, AND and OR. Control flow instructions change the sequence of execution, such as branches, jumps and calls. Input and output instructions transfer data to and from external devices. Some ISAs also provide specialised instructions for floating-point arithmetic, string handling or multimedia operations.

Addressing Modes

An addressing mode is the method used to locate an operand. In immediate addressing, the operand value itself is part of the instruction. In direct addressing, the instruction contains the memory address of the operand. In register addressing, the operand is held in a register named by the instruction. In indirect addressing, the instruction gives the address of a location that holds the address of the operand. In indexed addressing, an index register is added to a base address to compute the effective address, which is useful for accessing arrays.

ISA versus Microarchitecture

The distinction between ISA and microarchitecture is frequently examined. The ISA is what the programmer sees: the instructions, registers and memory model. The microarchitecture is how the processor is built to implement that ISA: its pipeline depth, cache sizes, branch prediction and execution units. Two processors can share the same ISA but have very different microarchitectures and therefore different speeds. Well-known ISAs include x86, ARM and MIPS.

bodyText:
What Pipelining Is

Pipelining is a technique in which the execution of an instruction is divided into stages, and different instructions are processed in different stages at the same time, like an assembly line. While one instruction is being executed, the next instruction is being decoded and the one after that is being fetched. Pipelining does not reduce the time taken by a single instruction, but it increases throughput, the number of instructions completed per unit of time, because several instructions are in progress at once.

The Five-Stage Pipeline

A classic RISC pipeline has five stages. In instruction fetch (IF), the instruction is fetched from memory. In instruction decode (ID), the instruction is decoded and registers are read. In execute (EX), the ALU performs the operation. In memory access (MEM), data memory is read or written if needed. In write back (WB), the result is written to a register. Ideally, one instruction completes every clock cycle once the pipeline is full, even though each instruction still takes five cycles from start to finish.

Pipeline Hazards

A pipeline hazard is a situation that prevents the next instruction from executing in its designated clock cycle. Structural hazards occur when two instructions need the same hardware resource at the same time. Data hazards occur when an instruction depends on the result of an earlier instruction that has not finished yet. Control hazards occur when a branch instruction makes it unclear which instruction should be fetched next. Common solutions include forwarding, where a result is passed directly to the next stage; stalling, where the pipeline is paused with a bubble; and branch prediction, where the processor guesses the outcome of a branch.

Parallel Processing

Parallel processing means carrying out several computations at the same time. Instruction-level parallelism (ILP) executes multiple instructions from one program simultaneously, for example through superscalar processors that issue more than one instruction per cycle. Thread-level and task-level parallelism run different threads or tasks on different cores. Multicore processors place two or more processor cores on a single chip. Amdahl's law states that the overall speedup of a program is limited by the fraction of the program that cannot be parallelised, so a large serial portion sharply limits the gain from adding processors.

Flynn's Taxonomy

Flynn's taxonomy, proposed by Michael J. Flynn in 1966, classifies computer architectures by the number of instruction streams and data streams. SISD is a single instruction stream operating on a single data stream, the traditional uniprocessor. SIMD is a single instruction stream operating on multiple data streams, used in vector processors and graphics processing. MISD, multiple instruction streams on a single data stream, is rare in practice. MIMD is multiple instruction streams on multiple data streams, the model of multicore and multiprocessor systems.

bodyText:
Why Cache Memory Exists

Cache memory is a small, fast memory placed between the processor and main memory. Processors operate much faster than main memory, so without cache the processor would constantly wait for data. Cache holds copies of frequently used instructions and data close to the processor, reducing average access time. Cache works because of locality of reference: temporal locality means data used recently is likely to be used again soon, and spatial locality means data near recently used data is likely to be used soon.

The Cache Hierarchy: L1, L2 and L3

Modern processors use several levels of cache in a hierarchy. Level 1 (L1) cache is the smallest and fastest, built directly into the processor core, and is usually split into separate instruction cache and data cache. Level 2 (L2) cache is larger and slower than L1, and is usually private to each core. Level 3 (L3) cache is the largest and slowest of the three, and is usually shared among all cores on the chip. When the processor needs data, it checks L1 first, then L2, then L3, and only then main memory. A cache hit means the data was found in cache; a cache miss means it was not and must be fetched from a lower level or main memory.

Cache Mapping Techniques

Cache mapping decides where a block of main memory can be placed in cache. In direct mapping, each main memory block maps to exactly one cache line, which is simple but can cause frequent conflicts. In fully associative mapping, a block can be placed in any cache line, which is flexible but expensive in hardware. In set-associative mapping, the cache is divided into sets, and a block can be placed in any line within its assigned set; this is the most common compromise in modern processors. When the cache is full and a new block must be loaded, a replacement policy such as least recently used (LRU) decides which existing block to evict.

Write Policies

When the processor writes data, the cache must stay consistent with main memory. In the write-through policy, data is written to both cache and main memory at the same time, which keeps memory up to date but is slower. In the write-back policy, data is written only to cache and is copied to main memory later, when the block is evicted; this is faster but requires a dirty bit to mark blocks that have been modified. Cache coherence is the related problem of keeping caches consistent across multiple cores, so that one core does not read stale data written by another.

bodyText:
Definitions

RISC stands for Reduced Instruction Set Computer, and CISC stands for Complex Instruction Set Computer. The two terms describe different philosophies for designing a processor's instruction set. RISC designs use a small set of simple instructions, each of which typically executes in one clock cycle. CISC designs use a larger set of more complex instructions, each of which can perform several operations and may take multiple clock cycles to complete. The distinction is a design philosophy, not a strict dividing line, and modern processors often blend features of both.

RISC Characteristics

RISC processors emphasise simplicity and speed of execution. They use fixed-length instructions that are easy to decode, a load-store architecture in which only LOAD and STORE instructions access memory while all other operations work on registers, and a large number of general-purpose registers. This simplicity makes pipelining efficient and allows higher clock speeds. The RISC concept was developed in the late 1970s and early 1980s, notably in the Berkeley RISC and Stanford MIPS projects. Well-known RISC architectures include ARM and MIPS.

CISC Characteristics

CISC processors emphasise powerful, complex instructions that reduce the number of instructions a program needs. They use variable-length instructions, many addressing modes, and instructions that can operate directly on memory. A single CISC instruction may, for example, load data, add it and store the result. This makes programs shorter and reduces the work of the compiler, but decoding is more complex and pipelining is harder. The best-known CISC architecture is x86, used in most desktop and laptop computers.

Comparison and Modern Practice

The practical trade-off is between simple instructions executed quickly and complex instructions that do more per instruction. RISC programs typically contain more instructions but each is simple and fast; CISC programs contain fewer instructions but each is more complex. In practice the boundary has blurred: modern x86 processors translate complex CISC instructions into simpler RISC-like micro-operations internally, while modern RISC designs such as ARM have added more complex instructions. ARM dominates mobile phones and embedded devices because of its power efficiency, while x86 remains dominant in desktop and server computing.
